name: Testosterone

lead: Testosterone is the principal male sex hormone, made mainly in the testes. It builds muscle and bone, drives body hair, voice deepening and the jaw and brow development of puberty, and it shapes the leaner, more masculine physique people associate with high levels.

It binds the androgen receptor, raising muscle protein synthesis, satellite cell activity and bone formation, and is partly converted to estradiol and DHT. It is prescribed as replacement therapy for diagnosed hypogonadism, where benefit is well documented. Healthy young men given supraphysiologic amounts gain muscle in a dose-dependent way, and anabolic steroid use is a staple of bodybuilding. Claims about changing facial structure in adults are mostly anecdotal.

paras: Medically it is delivered by injection, gel, patch or other forms under physician supervision, with blood monitoring, as replacement therapy. In physique circles it is discussed as TRT or as higher-level steroid use, usually combined with heavy training and diet. Muscle changes appear over weeks to months.

Prescription-only and a controlled substance in many countries. Documented risks include suppression of natural production and fertility, acne, polycythemia, blood pressure and lipid changes, mood effects and possible cardiovascular strain, and stopping abruptly can leave a deficiency. This entry is informational, not guidance for use.

chain: Leaner, more masculine physique and face
angle.text: Testosterone is the hormone behind muscle, jaw and brow development, body hair and voice, and it is used as replacement therapy (TRT) or at high levels for physique. More androgen signalling means more muscle and bone mass and a leaner, more masculine build. Muscle effects are well studied in medical and trial settings; claims about enhancing adult facial structure are mostly anecdotal.

lead: Testosterone is the principal male sex hormone and an androgen, a steroid hormone made mainly by the testicles in males and in smaller amounts by the ovaries in females. It drives the development of male reproductive tissues and secondary sexual characteristics, including increases in muscle and bone mass, body hair growth, voice deepening and remodelling of the jaw, brow and facial bone contours at puberty, and it also influences mood, libido, red blood cell production and metabolism.[1][2] In appearance terms, it is the hormone behind the physique and, through puberty, much of the facial structure that looksmaxxing communities discuss: broader shoulders, greater muscle mass, a squarer jaw and heavier brow, facial and body hair.

As a medicine, testosterone is prescribed as replacement therapy for male hypogonadism (a diagnosed deficiency), for gender dysphoria and for some breast cancers, and it appears on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines. It can be delivered by injection, skin gel or patch, cheek tablet, nasal gel, subdermal pellet or oral capsule.[1][3] Outside medicine, supraphysiologic doses are a staple of bodybuilding and physique culture, and testosterone is discussed on strength-training forums such as T Nation and on looksmaxxing forums, where members talk about both prescribed replacement and wider use of anabolic compounds.[4][5][6] Healthy young men given supraphysiologic testosterone gain muscle size and strength, especially with strength training, in controlled trials.[4][7]

Research supports benefit from replacement in men with true deficiency, with benefit most clearly documented for sexual function, and a large randomized trial in men with hypogonadism found no excess of major cardiovascular events over placebo.[8][9] Evidence for benefit from treating age-related decline in otherwise healthy men is less settled, and non-prescribed use at high doses is associated with documented harms including suppression of the body's own hormone production and fertility.[1][10][11]

Testosterone has also become a mass-media and social-media subject. Advertising of 'low T' in the 2000s and 2010s, and in the mid-2020s a 'T-maxxing' trend among young men, have been covered by news outlets and men's health bodies, which describe both lifestyle-based and drug-based attempts to raise testosterone.[12][13][14]

paras: Testosterone is a steroid of the androstane class that is built in several enzymatic steps from cholesterol, acts by binding and activating the androgen receptor, and is inactivated in the liver.[1] Production is regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: gonadotropin-releasing hormone prompts the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone, which stimulates testicular output, and rising testosterone feeds back to dampen the signal.[2] Levels follow a daily rhythm that peaks in the morning, and average adult male levels are several times those of adult females.[1][2]

Testosterone can act directly or after conversion by 5-alpha-reductase into dihydrotestosterone, which binds the androgen receptor more strongly, or by aromatase into estradiol. Its effects are traditionally described as anabolic (muscle mass and strength, bone density and strength, linear growth and bone maturation) and androgenic (maturation of the sex organs, voice deepening, facial and body hair), though the categories overlap considerably.[1]

Before birth, testosterone and its metabolite dihydrotestosterone contribute to the differentiation of male genitalia, and prenatal androgen exposure has been linked to sex-typed behaviour. In pubertal males, sustained rises in androgen are associated with growth of the jaw, brow, chin and nose and remodelling of facial bone contours (in conjunction with growth hormone), broadening of the shoulders, expansion of the rib cage, laryngeal growth, increased sebaceous gland activity and acne.[1] These pubertal changes are the reason testosterone is often discussed in appearance-focused communities.

In adults, testosterone supports spermatogenesis, libido, red blood cell production, muscle and bone maintenance and fat distribution, and levels drift down with age, by roughly one percent a year after about age 30 according to one summary.[1][2] Low levels in men are associated with frailty, fat accumulation, depressed mood, sexual dysfunction and bone loss, whereas excessive levels have been associated with hyperandrogenism and male-pattern hair loss.[1] Low testosterone has also been associated with higher inflammatory markers, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk, and studies of cognition describe a curved relationship in which both too little and too much circulating androgen may impair spatial performance.[1]

Wikipedia describes pubertal testosterone as contributing to growth of the jaw, brow, chin and nose and remodelling of facial bone contours, in conjunction with growth hormone, along with facial hair growth and increased sebaceous gland activity and acne.[1] A study of adolescent faces rated by women found that features such as a broader forehead, chin, jaw and nose most reliably signalled male identity, and the features that cued maleness were associated with plasma testosterone beyond the effect of age.[15]

Studies of adults link facial masculinity to hormone exposure earlier in life. A 20-year follow-up of 183 people found that higher testosterone in umbilical cord blood at birth was associated with more masculinised facial features in adulthood.[16] A study of men's responses to a competition found that men with more masculine facial structure showed higher testosterone after winning, while noting that clear evidence for a link between circulating adult testosterone and face shape had been absent.[17] The facial width-to-height ratio, a measure popularised in online discussion, was not associated with testosterone in a sample of adolescent Tsimane males in a 2016 study.[18] In a perception study, women with higher estradiol showed stronger preferences for faces of men with higher testosterone.[19] None of these studies tested adult administration of testosterone against facial structure.

Testosterone raises fat-free mass and muscle size and lowers fat mass in a dose-dependent way in healthy young men; in a 1996 randomized study of 43 men, supraphysiologic weekly injections of testosterone enanthate increased muscle size and strength, with the largest gains in men who also lifted weights.[7] The graded dose-response study of Bhasin and colleagues found fat-free mass, leg press strength, leg power and muscle volume rose with testosterone concentration while fat mass fell.[4]

The same hormone has less welcome cosmetic effects. Wikipedia lists acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss and gynecomastia at high doses among common effects of testosterone medication, and describes male pattern baldness as linked to excessive androgen exposure.[1][20] A looksmax.org thread title lists TRT alongside an aromatase inhibitor, finasteride and dutasteride, the latter two being medicines for hair loss.[21]

Testosterone replacement therapy aims to restore serum levels to the normal range in men with symptomatic deficiency, targeting reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, low mood, anaemia and loss of muscle and bone mass. Narrative reviews note that therapy has been in use for about seventy years and that many formulations (buccal, nasal, subdermal, transdermal and intramuscular) have been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and adherence.[3][22] Testosterone is also used in gender-affirming hormone therapy and for delayed puberty in boys.[1]

Guidelines from the American College of Physicians (2020) support discussing treatment in men with age-related low testosterone who have sexual dysfunction, with yearly review and discontinuation if there is no improvement. Whether testosterone for low levels due to ageing alone is beneficial or harmful is described as unclear in the broader literature.[1]

Healthy young men given supraphysiologic testosterone gain muscle in a dose-dependent manner, a finding established in controlled dose-response work and the basis of anabolic steroid use in bodybuilding.[4] In the looksmaxxing and physique communities, testosterone is discussed both as medically supervised 'TRT' and as a component of non-prescribed 'cycles' for muscle, leanness and what users describe as improved drive and confidence. Medical reviews of non-prescribed anabolic steroid use report that complications vary by dose, duration and compound and that users may develop symptomatic hypogonadism afterward.[10]

In 1849 Arnold Adolph Berthold transplanted testes in castrated cockerels and observed that the birds kept their male behaviour, leading him to propose that the testes act through the blood; the work was largely ignored for decades.[23] In 1889 Charles-Edouard Brown-Sequard published self-experiments injecting testicular extracts in The Lancet and reported a surge of strength and energy; a historical review says the effects were most likely placebo, but the report fuelled a wave of commercial organotherapy products.[23]

In 1935 testosterone was isolated and synthesised by several groups: Ernst Laqueur's group in Amsterdam isolated about 10 mg from 100 kg of bull testes and named it testosterone, while Adolf Butenandt and G. Hanisch in Gottingen and Leopold Ruzicka and A. Wettstein in Basel published chemical syntheses. 17-alpha-methyltestosterone, which is orally active, was synthesised in the same year and later found to be liver-toxic.[23] Wikipedia dates the medical use of testosterone from 1939.[20]

Testosterone was first given as subcutaneous pellets because it was ineffective by mouth; from the mid-1950s the longer-acting injectable testosterone enanthate became standard. From the 1950s onward, pharmaceutical research tried to separate anabolic from androgenic effects, describing 256 androgenic steroids by 1956 and more than 1,000 by 1976 without a clean separation.[23] Wikipedia's anabolic steroid article says AAS were synthesised in the 1930s and used for many purposes by physicians, and that from the mid-1980s the media reported 'roid rage'.[24]

Athletes' use led to regulation. After Ben Johnson's 1988 Olympic case drove stricter controls, the US passed the Anabolic Steroid Control Act in 1990, making testosterone a controlled substance (Schedule III).[20] The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as prohibited at all times.[1] A 1996 review estimated over one million past or current US steroid users, and the article cites 1 to 3 million as a common estimate, most of them non-competitive bodybuilders or non-athletes by one survey.[24]

US testosterone use rose from 0.5% of men in 2002 to 3.2% in 2013 and fell to 1.7% in 2016, according to a JAMA analysis summarised by Wikipedia, while UK prescriptions nearly doubled from 2000 to 2010.[25] A 2014 analysis of US and UK records from 2000 to 2011 found testing and treatment had increased pronouncedly in the US, that many US men started treatment with normal levels, and that gels had become the most common initial treatment; its authors urged prescribers to consider medical necessity before initiating.[12] The FDA announced an investigation of cardiovascular risks in January 2014, and changed labelling in March 2015 to warn of possible increased heart attack and stroke risk.[25] After TRAVERSE reported in 2023, the FDA revised the labelling in February 2025, with Wikipedia describing removal of the boxed cardiovascular warning and an added warning about increased blood pressure.[20][25]
A large body of human research exists for testosterone, mostly in men with hypogonadism or low testosterone. This section summarises landmark and illustrative studies.

Dose-response: In a controlled study of healthy young men given graded weekly doses, testosterone produced dose-dependent increases in fat-free mass and muscle size, with strength and power changes also related to dose, while the men's own gonadal output was suppressed.[4]

Older hypogonadal men: A 12-month randomized trial of testosterone replacement in older hypogonadal men examined changes in body composition and related measures.[26] A trial in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes reported improved insulin resistance, glycaemic control, visceral adiposity and cholesterol with replacement.[27] Replacement in hypogonadal men has also been associated with changes in inflammatory cytokines and lipid profiles.[28]

Sexual function and symptoms: A randomized trial in men with hypogonadism reported on sexual function and hypogonadal symptoms during testosterone therapy compared with placebo, with improvements in sexual function being the best-documented effect.[9]

Cardiovascular safety: The TRAVERSE trial, a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled non-inferiority trial, enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with symptoms of hypogonadism, two low testosterone readings, and either existing or high risk of cardiovascular disease. It was designed to test whether testosterone replacement caused more major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo.[8] Wikipedia notes that a randomized trial found no evidence of excess major adverse cardiac events versus placebo in men with low testosterone.[1] In TRAVERSE, a primary cardiovascular event occurred in 7.0% of the testosterone group and 7.3% of the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.96), meeting the non-inferiority criterion; mean follow-up was 33 months.[8]

Prostate safety: A randomized clinical trial published in JAMA Network Open compared testosterone with placebo for high-grade prostate cancer, any prostate cancer, acute urinary retention, invasive prostate procedures and drug treatment for urinary symptoms in men with hypogonadism.[29] A systematic review focused on men with previous or active localized prostate cancer has also examined this question.[30] Wikipedia's summary is that testosterone does not appear to increase the risk of developing prostate cancer, whereas raising testosterone above castrate levels has been shown to speed progression of existing prostate cancer in men on androgen deprivation.[1]

Fertility: A 2025 review concluded that exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropins and intratesticular testosterone and so impairs spermatogenesis; sperm production often resumes slowly after cessation but with highly variable timing, and exogenous testosterone is contraindicated in men trying to conceive.[11]

Registered trials: ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of testosterone replacement in heart failure patients with exercise training, in men with dysthymia, in advanced-cancer fatigue, in low-risk hormone-refractory prostate cancer, in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and in delayed puberty, among others.[31][32][33][34]

Supraphysiologic dosing in normal men: In 1996 Bhasin and colleagues randomly assigned 43 healthy men to testosterone enanthate or placebo, with or without weight training, for 10 weeks; men given testosterone without exercise gained triceps area versus a loss on placebo, and men given testosterone plus exercise gained the most fat-free mass and strength.[7]

Older men: The Testosterone Trials randomized 790 men aged 65 and over with low testosterone and symptoms to testosterone gel or placebo for a year; treatment raised testosterone to the mid-normal range of young men and produced moderate benefit in sexual function and some benefit in mood and depressive symptoms, but not in vitality or walking distance, and the trial was too small to assess risks.[35]

Diabetes prevention: The T4DM trial randomized 1,007 overweight men aged 50 to 74 with low-normal testosterone and impaired glucose tolerance or early type 2 diabetes, all in a lifestyle programme, to injections of testosterone undecanoate or placebo for 2 years; diabetes by glucose tolerance test occurred in 12% on testosterone versus 21% on placebo (relative risk 0.59).[36]

Guidelines: The Endocrine Society's 2018 guideline recommends diagnosing hypogonadism only in men with symptoms and signs of deficiency and consistently low morning fasting testosterone, and recommends against starting therapy in men planning near-term fertility or with breast or prostate cancer, among other conditions.[37] The American College of Physicians 2020 guideline is summarised above.[20]

Common side effects of testosterone medication include acne, fluid retention and breast enlargement in males; more serious effects described include liver toxicity (mainly with oral alkylated androgens, which narrative reviews say should be avoided), cardiovascular concerns, polycythemia and behavioural changes.[1][22] Accidental exposure can virilise women and children, the drug is advised against in men with prostate cancer, and it can cause harm in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1]

Exogenous testosterone causes reversible suppression of spermatogenesis, and clinicians who treat deficiency in men wanting future fertility describe adjuncts such as human chorionic gonadotropin, selective estrogen receptor modulators or aromatase inhibitors.[22][11] A review of anabolic steroid-induced hypogonadism reports that symptomatic hypogonadism can follow non-prescribed androgen use, depending on dose, duration and compound, and that managing it may involve carefully judged replacement therapy, hCG and SERMs.[10]

Wikipedia lists pulmonary oil microembolism among reactions to some injectable products, polycythemia and worsened sleep apnoea among blood and sleep effects, and notes that PSA usually rises on therapy.[25] It notes one TRAVERSE analysis found atrial fibrillation at 3.5% versus 2.4% with placebo, which other analyses did not confirm.[25] For non-prescribed use, the anabolic steroid article lists unfavourable cholesterol changes, high blood pressure, left ventricular hypertrophy, suppressed natural testosterone, testicular atrophy, reduced sperm production, gynecomastia, aggression and, in adolescents, premature closure of growth plates; the IARC lists anabolic steroids in Group 2A as probably carcinogenic to humans.[24]

Healthy Male, an Australian men's health organisation, says taking testosterone shuts off natural production, with recovery taking weeks to months after stopping, and lists dependence and withdrawal symptoms such as low mood and fatigue.[14]

Approved preparations are delivered by injection, skin delivery, buccal or nasal routes or oral formulations, and reviews compare these options by pharmacokinetics and adverse effects, and note that all approved methods, used as recommended, can restore normal serum concentrations in most hypogonadal men.[3][22][38]

Physiologically, testosterone is made in Leydig cells under luteinizing hormone control, with cholesterol conversion to pregnenolone as the rate-limiting step, and a portion is converted peripherally to dihydrotestosterone and estradiol.[2]
Testosterone is a prescription-only drug, and a controlled substance in many jurisdictions, with generic products available for approved indications.[1]
Wikipedia lists the drug as Schedule III in the US, Class C in the UK and Schedule IV in Canada, and notes that the Nevada athletic commission banned TRT for UFC fighters in February 2014.[20][25]

subs.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: On T Nation, testosterone is discussed in dedicated 'TRT' threads, by users who report being diagnosed hypogonadal and treated for years, and in broader 'gear' discussions of stacked steroid regimens.[5][39] Some members describe competing in a 'natural' federation that allows TRT, saying the physique they reached was attainable without supraphysiologic levels.[5][39] Others in the same community argue that testosterone mainly amplifies existing traits rather than creating them, with one commenter likening the effect to a multiplier on what is there naturally.[40]

Newsweek and the Australian organisation Healthy Male describe 'T-maxxing' as a social media trend, aimed mostly at young men, of trying to raise testosterone to build muscle, confidence and masculinity, which Healthy Male says grew out of the manosphere alongside looksmaxxing and gymmaxxing.[13][14] Lifestyle habits promoted include sleep, zone 2 cardio and cutting back on doom-scrolling, while Healthy Male describes ice baths and raw onions as useless and self-injection of unprescribed testosterone as dangerous.[13][14] Newsweek quotes Utah urologist Alexander Pastuszak saying social media has made testosterone a "proxy for masculinity and vitality," and that treatment without need can create dependence on a therapy never needed.[13]

On looksmax.org, threads discuss starting long-term TRT in the late teens or early twenties, adding anti-oestrogen and hCG protocols and cruising versus blasting, with titles such as one arguing moderate TRT does not age you aesthetically.[6][41][42] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places off-label use of substances such as peptides and weight-loss drugs under hardmaxxing.[43]

Testosterone sits alongside other androgen-linked and body-composition topics in the wiki: anabolic steroids more broadly, aromatase and DHT management, finasteride and dutasteride for hair, and supplements marketed as testosterone boosters, including combinations of boron, zinc and vitamin D, which have no published trial as a stack.

lore.intro: On strength-training forums such as T Nation, testosterone is discussed as a medical therapy ('TRT'), as a component of non-prescribed cycles, and as a determinant of physique and appearance.[5][40] On looksmax.org, threads discuss starting TRT in the late teens or early twenties and describe it as part of an aesthetic regimen.[6][42] News and health organisations describe a 'T-maxxing' trend among young men.[13][14]

claims.claim: TRT is a legitimate long-term treatment that restores wellbeing in men with diagnosed low testosterone
Testosterone amplifies a man's existing traits ('a multiplier') rather than creating new ones
Supraphysiologic testosterone reliably builds muscle in healthy men
TRT is compatible with 'natural' bodybuilding and attainable without drugs at supraphysiologic levels
Testosterone treatment is safe for the heart and prostate
Young men without a deficiency should start TRT for life to look better.
Testosterone reshapes the adult face, jaw and brow.
Natural habits can raise testosterone enough to matter (T-maxxing).
Testosterone injections can be stopped without lasting effects.
